touches.text: Code that is no longer needed is deleted. Git history keeps it if we ever need it back.
Two callers waking the same part at once start only one: the part that binds its socket first is the only one; a second copy finds it taken and exits quietly (as the ground loop does, 5.6.4.3).
ANTI-INTENTION: what it must never grow back: a bus, a shim, probes, other kinds of pulses, staleness, managers.
A second copy refuses to start.
It launches each device's cairn/devices/<device>/groundloop/pulse.py, each as its own process (5.8.3.4).
It writes one JSON record at the end of a pass listing each device: beat time, device folder found or NOT FOUND, file mtime, pid spawned. It does no checks and no takeover.

Beat interval is a setting, 60 s for now, expected to go a lot faster ("faster than once a second") now that nothing heavy hangs off it. So the scheduler fires an entry whose time fell since the last beat, not one that equals the beat's minute: any beat length fires each entry exactly once.
"Is it up?" is the rack's to answer. A device that doesn't respond within about 30 seconds, while the CPU isn't pegged and slowing it down, MIGHT be a candidate for killing and restarting.

base shim: the base class for every shim, customized for the device it interfaces with, internal or external. Carries the panes every device has (2.3.8), the scheduler (5.9), and the [all] verbs (2.4.11.2).

conflicts.text: It writes one JSON record at the end of a pass listing each device: beat time, device folder found or NOT FOUND, file mtime, pid spawned. It does no checks and no takeover.
conflicts.ticket_says: The ground loop writes beat.json containing only its own state: timestamp (now), pid, and state. No per-device information is recorded.
conflicts.why: The outline prescribes: 'It writes one JSON record at the end of a pass listing each device: beat time, device folder found or NOT FOUND, file mtime, pid spawned.' The ticket's beat.json omits the per-device telemetry entirely. The outline says the record must list each device; the ticket does not. Both cannot stand as written—the outline requires device enumeration in the loop's record, the ticket moves device tracking to the rack exclusively and gives the loop only its own heartbeat.

conflicts.text: There is no central supervisor. Each part starts what it needs by trying to use it: sending a message starts the bus if it is down, a message arriving wakes its shim, the shim wakes its device. Many very small supervisors, each one detect-and-start. WHY: a supervisor is one more thing to keep up, and the system must come up from any part that is touched.
conflicts.ticket_says: The singleton lock in cairn/tools/base/singleton.py detects liveness of the ground loop by testing whether the lock is held. Base shim ensure_ground_loop probes this lock and returns 'up: True' when held, spawning nothing.
conflicts.why: The outline section 5.3.5 describes how the waker works: 'Every client's connect is a wake attempt' (5.3.5.1); 'the part that binds its socket first is the only one' (5.3.5.2). But the ground loop no longer uses the waker to start itself (it starts on its own and claims a lock). The outline prescribes that two callers waking the same part result in one binding its socket and the other exiting quietly—the traditional TCP/UDS binding race. The ticket replaces this with an explicit lock file that the loop holds, changing the startup race from socket-binding to file-lock-claiming. Section 5.3.5 describes the waker's role; the ticket sidesteps it for the loop.
